slides.title: Network troubleshooting
slides.sub: Domain 5: the heaviest domain on the exam
slides.say: Welcome to domain five of the Network Plus N10-009 exam: network troubleshooting. At twenty-four percent, this is the heaviest domain, so it is worth the most points. We will cover the troubleshooting methodology, cabling and interface problems, service problems, performance problems, and the tools you use to find them.

slides.title: 5.1 The seven-step methodology
steps: Gather info, question users, ask what changed
Confirmed? Move on. Not? New theory or escalate
Make the fix, or hand it off
slides.callout: Always the same order. Always ask what changed first.
slides.say: The methodology has seven steps, always in the same order. One, identify the problem. Gather information, question users, find out what changed, duplicate the problem if you can, and handle multiple problems individually. Two, establish a theory of probable cause, and question the obvious first. Three, test the theory. If it is confirmed, move on. If not, make a new theory or escalate. Four, establish a plan of action and identify the possible effects. Five, implement the solution, or escalate. Six, verify full system functionality and put preventive measures in place. Seven, document your findings, actions, and outcomes. Exam questions love to ask which step comes next, so memorize the order.

slides.title: Choosing an approach
items: Top-down: start at the Application layer and work down
Bottom-up: start at the Physical layer and work up
Divide and conquer: start in the middle, for example with ping, then go up or down
Follow the path: trace the route the traffic takes
Compare with a known good device, and change one thing at a time
slides.say: When you build your theory, you can choose an approach. Top-down starts at the application layer and works down. Bottom-up starts at the physical layer and works up. Divide and conquer starts in the middle, for example with a ping, and then moves up or down depending on the result. You can also follow the path the traffic takes, or compare against a device that works. Whatever you do, change only one thing at a time so you know what fixed the problem.

slides.title: 5.2 Interface states
head: What you see
Most likely cause
rows: Bad or unplugged cable, wrong cable type, dead far end
Layer 2 problem: mismatch, encapsulation, or the far end
A protection feature tripped, such as port security or BPDU guard
Speed or duplex mismatch, or bad cabling
slides.say: Now objective five point two: cabling and interface problems. Read the interface state carefully. Down and down usually means a bad or unplugged cable, the wrong cable type, or a dead device at the far end. Up and down means the signal is there but layer two is not working, which points to a mismatch or the far end. Administratively down means someone ran the shutdown command. Err-disabled means a protection feature, such as port security or B P D U guard, shut the port. And C R C errors or late collisions point to a duplex or speed mismatch, or bad cabling.

slides.title: Cable and transceiver problems
items: Attenuation and distance: copper runs are limited to 100 meters
Crosstalk and EMI: keep copper away from power and motors
Transceiver mismatch: wrong type, speed, or wavelength
Single-mode and multimode fiber cannot be mixed
Dirty or bent fiber loses light; test with a visual fault locator
PoE problems: the power budget is exceeded
slides.say: Physical problems have a short list of causes. Attenuation means the signal weakens with distance, and copper is limited to one hundred meters. Crosstalk and E M I come from interference, so keep copper away from power cables and motors. A transceiver mismatch, meaning the wrong type, speed, or wavelength, will keep a link down, and single-mode and multimode fiber cannot be mixed. Dirty or sharply bent fiber loses light, and a visual fault locator shows you where. With Power over Ethernet, the switch can simply run out of power budget.

slides.title: 5.3 Addressing and DHCP problems
head: Symptom
Likely cause
rows: Port is in the wrong VLAN
DHCP pool exhausted, or no DHCP reply
Wrong gateway or DNS you did not set
Rogue DHCP server; use DHCP snooping
Works on the subnet, nowhere else
Works by IP, fails by name
slides.say: Objective five point three covers network services. If a host gets an address from the wrong scope, its switch port is in the wrong V LAN. If new clients get addresses starting with one sixty-nine dot two fifty-four, the D H C P pool is exhausted or the server did not answer. If clients receive a gateway or D N S server you never configured, suspect a rogue D H C P server, and use D H C P snooping. If a host works on its own subnet but nowhere else, check the default gateway. If it works by I P but fails by name, it is D N S. And two hosts with intermittent loss can mean a duplicate I P address.

slides.title: Routing and switching faults
items: MTU mismatch: small packets pass, large ones drop
Routing loop: packets circle until the TTL hits zero
Asymmetric routing: replies return on a different path
Native VLAN mismatch: untagged frames land in the wrong VLAN
STP: root port, designated port, alternate port blocks the loop
An ACL or firewall rule blocks one port while others work
slides.say: Some faults live in routing and switching. An M T U mismatch lets small packets pass while large ones are dropped. A routing loop sends packets in circles until the T T L reaches zero. Asymmetric routing sends replies back on a different path, and stateful devices may drop them. A native V LAN mismatch on a trunk puts untagged frames in the wrong V LAN. In spanning tree, know the port roles: the root port, designated ports, and the alternate port that blocks to stop a loop. And when one port fails while others work, check the A C L or firewall rules.

slides.title: 5.4 Performance problems
items: Congestion and saturation: bandwidth is used up
Latency, jitter, and packet loss: hurt voice and video most
Wireless: interference, weak signal, channel overlap
Client disassociation: weak signal, roaming, or authentication
Too many clients on one access point
Fixes: QoS, more channels, move or add access points
slides.say: Objective five point four is performance. Congestion happens when bandwidth is used up. Latency, jitter, and packet loss hurt voice and video first. On wireless, the usual culprits are interference, weak signal, and overlapping channels. Repeated disassociation messages mean the client's signal is too weak or noisy, or that roaming or authentication is failing. Too many clients on one access point also slows everyone down. Typical fixes are Q o S, cleaner channels, and moving or adding access points.

slides.title: 5.5 Software tools
head: Tool
What it tells you
slides.say: Objective five point five is the toolbox. Ping tests reachability with I C M P. Trace R T or traceroute shows each hop on the path. N S lookup and dig show D N S answers. I P config, if config, or the I P command show a host's address settings. A R P shows the mapping from I P to mac addresses. Net stat lists connections and listening ports. N map scans a host for open ports. And T C P dump or Wireshark captures packets so you can see exactly what is on the wire.

slides.title: Device commands and hardware tools
items: show interface: state, errors, speed and duplex
show vlan and show config: verify the setup
show power inline: PoE budget
LLDP is vendor neutral; CDP is Cisco only
Cable tester and loopback adapter: check copper
Tone generator and probe: trace a cable
OTDR and visual fault locator: find fiber breaks
slides.say: On network devices, show interface gives the state, errors, speed, and duplex. Show V LAN and show config verify the setup, and show power inline shows the Power over Ethernet budget. L L D P is the vendor-neutral neighbor discovery protocol, while C D P is Cisco only. For hardware, use a cable tester or loopback adapter on copper, a tone generator and probe to trace a cable, and an O T D R or visual fault locator to find breaks in fiber.

slides.title: Domain 5 recap
items: Seven steps in order, starting with what changed
Read the interface state before you guess
Match the symptom to the cause: VLAN, DHCP, DNS, gateway, MTU
Pick the tool that answers the question
Verify, then document
slides.say: To recap domain five: know the seven steps in order, and always start with what changed. Read the interface state before you guess. Match the symptom to its cause, whether that is the V LAN, D H C P, D N S, the gateway, or M T U. Pick the tool that answers the question you are asking. And finish by verifying the fix and documenting it. Good luck.
